deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics. It is part of an introductory history lecture or school notebook (Weltgeschichte), continuing from the previous page's account of how civilization spread from Asia to Africa to Europe.

Content, in order:
(1) End of the argument on the origin of government. People had to give one person more authority to uphold the laws. They usually preferred those who had distinguished themselves by experience and prudence. This is how authorities (Obrigkeiten), realms and governments arose.
(2) The standard threefold periodization of world history:
- Ancient history: from the Creation to the fall of the Western Roman Empire, given as 486 p.C.
- Middle history: from then to the discovery of America, 1492.
- Modern history: from then to the present.
(3) Geography and chronology are named as the chief auxiliary sciences of history. Two chronological systems are described: counting by years of the world (Anno Mundi) or by years before/after the birth of Christ. The Anno Mundi era is called unreliable and inconvenient: the numbers grow large and the uncertainties accumulate. The B.C./A.D. reckoning is called more convenient and more certain.
(4) A syllabus for ancient history:
- a. the oldest Asian and African realms, up to the rise of the Persian monarchy, 555 a.C.
- b. the Persian monarchy, to 333 a.C.
- c. the Greek states, up to Alexander, 333 a.C.
- d. the Macedonian monarchy, from 333 (written 'p. C.').
- e. the Romans.
(5) Heading of Section 1: history of the oldest Asian and African realms (continued on the next page as 'vor Cyrus': Assyrians, Medes, Babylonians).

There are no derivations or computations. The only numbers are dates. The handwriting and content suggest school or lecture notes, probably not Gauss's own work, filed in this bundle.
errors: The fall of the Western Roman Empire is conventionally dated 476 A.D. The page gives 486; this could be a slip, or 486 (Clovis's defeat of Syagrius) may be meant.
'Geschichte der macedonischen Monarchie 333 p. C.' should read 333 a. C. (B.C.); the Macedonian monarchy under Alexander begins in the 330s B.C.
555 B.C. for the start of the Persian monarchy (Cyrus) matches older textbook chronologies. Modern dating puts Cyrus's accession c. 559 B.C. and the conquest of Media c. 550 B.C.

The argument against Anno Mundi reckoning is garbled as written ('je weiter man seit Christi Geburt weiter vergrößern sich die Zahlen'); the intended sense is that the numbers become large and the uncertain epoch makes it unreliable.

results.what: Tripartite periodization of world history (ancient / medieval / modern), with 476/486 and 1492 as boundaries
results.usually_credited_to: Christoph Cellarius (late 17th c.); standard in 18th-century German schoolbooks (Schlözer, Gatterer)

results.what: Geography and chronology as auxiliary sciences; preference for B.C./A.D. over Anno Mundi reckoning
results.modern_name: Historical auxiliary sciences (Hilfswissenschaften); Dionysian era vs. Anno Mundi

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds only routine history-lesson content (periodization, chronology, syllabus) and no mathematics. It is most likely school or lecture notes, possibly not even in Gauss's hand.

transcription_corrections: Line 1: read 'zog man gewöhnlich die, [welche] durch Erfahrung und Klugheit sich auszeichneten, vor' — the '[?]' marks can be dropped; 'vor' is legible at the line end.
'Untergang des west-römischen Reichs. 486 p.C.' — the image indeed shows 486, not 476.
'd. Geschichte der macedonischen Monarchie 333 p. C.' — the image appears to show 'p. C.', which is a slip for a. C.
'Ungewissheiten' is more likely spelled 'Ungewißheiten' in the original.
